\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can introduce myself in Marathi, give my name, and understand the other person's name.}

Complete MR-C02-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise: introduce myself in Marathi, give my name, and understand the other person's name.

\section[nāv]{\mr{नाव} (nāv) — \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} a word older than Europe}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-naav}



\begin{quote}
To introduce yourself you need one word first: \textbf{name}. In Marathi it is \textbf{\mr{नाव}} (\emph{nāv}) — and it is a very old word wearing a Marathi coat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{ना}} (\emph{nā}, the \mr{न} \emph{na} with the \textbf{\mr{ा}} long-\emph{ā} stroke) + \textbf{\mr{व}} (\emph{va}) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{नाव}} \emph{nāv}. Two letters, read left to right.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{नाव}} (\emph{nāv}) comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{नामन्}} (\emph{nāman}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}). Watch the small Marathi sound-shift: the Sanskrit \emph{-m-} softened to \emph{-v-}, so \emph{nām} became \textbf{nāv}. (Hindi kept the \emph{m}: \emph{nām}.) That Sanskrit \emph{nāman} traces back to the same ancient root, \textbf{*h\textsubscript{3}nómn} — that final \emph{n} is syllabic, a consonant doing a vowel's work — that gave English \textbf{name} and \textbf{noun}, Latin \emph{nōmen}, Greek \emph{onoma}. A cousin from before either language had a name for itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Marathi softens many old Sanskrit consonants this way — \emph{m} leaning to \emph{v}, hard sounds going soft. Spotting the shift lets you read a Sanskrit word straight into its Marathi form.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāv\textquotedblright{} — name
  \item the English cousin from the same root (\textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{nāv}, and what happened to the \emph{m} of Sanskrit \emph{nām}? (\textquotedblleft{}Name\textquotedblright{}; it softened to \emph{v} — a Marathi sound-shift.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mājhaṁ]{\mr{माझं} (mājhaṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-majhe}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}My name.\textquotedblright{} The word for \textbf{my} — and it changes shape with the gender of what it owns.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{मा}} (\emph{mā}) + \textbf{\mr{झं}} (\emph{jhaṁ}, the \mr{झ} \emph{jha} with an \emph{anusvara} \textbf{\mr{ं}} for the light nasal) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{माझं}} \emph{mājhaṁ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{माझं}} (\emph{mājhaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) sits on the first-person root \textbf{ma-} — the very root behind English \textbf{me, my, mine}, Latin \emph{meus}, and Hindi \emph{merā}. One tiny syllable, \emph{ma}, marks \textquotedblleft{}belonging to me\textquotedblright{} across the whole Indo-European family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} agrees in three genders}]
Marathi keeps \textbf{three} genders, and \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} picks its ending from the noun: \textbf{\mr{माझा}} (\emph{mājhā}, masculine) · \textbf{\mr{माझी}} (\emph{mājhī}, feminine) · \textbf{\mr{माझं}} (\emph{mājhaṁ}, neuter). The word \textbf{\mr{नाव}} (\emph{nāv}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{neuter}, so \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\mr{माझं} \mr{नाव}} (\emph{mājhaṁ nāv}). You met this gender-agreement idea already with the goodbye \emph{yeto/yete}; it runs through the whole language.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mājhā / mājhī / mājhaṁ\textquotedblright{} — the three genders of \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mājhaṁ nāv\textquotedblright{} — my name (neuter, to match \emph{nāv})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} \emph{mājhaṁ nāv} and not \emph{mājhā nāv}? (\emph{nāv} is neuter, so \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} takes the neuter form \emph{mājhaṁ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āhe]{\mr{आहे} (āhe) — \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-aahe}



\begin{quote}
The little verb that finishes almost every Marathi sentence about what something \textbf{is} — and, in Marathi, it comes \textbf{last}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{आ}} (\emph{ā}, the standalone long-\emph{ā} vowel, used when a word begins with a vowel) + \textbf{\mr{हे}} (\emph{he}) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{आहे}} \emph{āhe}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{आहे}} (\emph{āhe}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) descends from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{अस्ति}} (\emph{ásti}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}), on the root \textbf{√as} (\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}). That same \emph{√as} / PIE \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}es-} is the ancestor of Latin \emph{est}, German \emph{ist}, and English \textbf{is} itself — the deepest, oldest verb in the family, worn down to \emph{āhe} in Marathi.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb goes last}]
Marathi is a \textbf{subject–object–verb} language: \textquotedblleft{}my name Mira \textbf{is}.\textquotedblright{} The copula \textbf{\mr{आहे}} sits at the \textbf{end}, where English puts it in the middle. It changes with the subject — you will meet \textbf{\mr{आहेस}} (\emph{āhes}, \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\mr{आहात}} (\emph{āhāt}, \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} respectful) in the next chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āhe\textquotedblright{} — is
  \item the English cousin from the same root (\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{āhe} sit in a Marathi sentence, and what English word is its cousin? (At the \textbf{end}; English \textbf{is}, both from \emph{√as}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mājhaṁ nāv … āhe]{\mr{माझं} \mr{नाव} … \mr{आहे} (mājhaṁ nāv … āhe) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-majhe-naav-aahe}



\begin{quote}
Now assemble the three atoms you just met into your first full sentence about yourself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the phrase, assembled}
\textbf{\mr{माझं}} (\emph{mājhaṁ}, my) + \textbf{\mr{नाव}} (\emph{nāv}, name) + \textbf{{[}your name{]}} + \textbf{\mr{आहे}} (\emph{āhe}, is) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{माझं} \mr{नाव} \mr{मीरा} \mr{आहे}} (\emph{mājhaṁ nāv Mīrā āhe}) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is Mira.\textquotedblright{}

Notice the shape:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{माझं}} is neuter, agreeing with the neuter \textbf{\mr{नाव}}.
  \item The verb \textbf{\mr{आहे}} comes \textbf{last} — \textquotedblleft{}my name Mira is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

A man or a woman says it the same way here; the gender lived in \emph{mājhaṁ} (matching \emph{nāv}), which is settled.

\begin{culture}
Marathi drops nothing and reorders everything to English eyes: possessor, thing, value, then \emph{is}. Learn this frame and you can swap in any name — or, later, any fact about yourself.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mājhaṁ nāv Mīrā āhe\textquotedblright{} — my name is Mira
  \item it with your own name in the blank
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Put \textquotedblleft{}my name is Arun\textquotedblright{} into Marathi. (\emph{mājhaṁ nāv Arun āhe.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tū / tumhī]{\mr{तू} / \mr{तुम्ही} (tū / tumhī) — \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-tu-tumhi}



\begin{quote}
Before you can ask someone \emph{their} name, you need \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — and Marathi gives you two, one warm, one respectful.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{तू}} (\emph{tū}, the \mr{त} \emph{ta} with the long-\emph{u} stroke \textbf{\mr{ू}}). And \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही}} (\emph{tumhī}): \textbf{\mr{तु}} + \textbf{\mr{म्ही}} (\emph{mhī}, the \mr{म} \emph{ma} with a \emph{halant} joining \mr{ह} \emph{ha}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{तू}} (\emph{tū}, familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{त्वम्}} (\emph{tvam}), from PIE \textbf{*tū} — the very root of English archaic \textbf{thou}, Latin \emph{tū}, French \emph{tu}, and Hindi \emph{tū}. The respectful \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही}} (\emph{tumhī}) is grammatically \textbf{plural}: you honour one person by addressing them as many, exactly as French does with \emph{vous}. It takes the plural verb \textbf{\mr{आहात}} (\emph{āhāt}), not \emph{āhes}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}s, a choice of respect}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{तू}} (\emph{tū}) — a friend, a child, someone close.
  \item \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही}} (\emph{tumhī}) — an elder, a stranger, anyone you show courtesy to.
\end{itemize}

Choosing between them is a small act of politeness Marathi makes you perform every time you speak to someone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tū\textquotedblright{} (close) / \textquotedblleft{}tumhī\textquotedblright{} (respectful)
  \item the English cousin of \emph{tū} (\textquotedblleft{}thou\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} for a teacher, and why? (\emph{tumhī} — the respectful plural, courtesy-by-plural like French \emph{vous}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāy]{\mr{काय} (kāy) — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-kaay}



\begin{quote}
One more atom before the question \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{} — the word \textbf{what} itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{का}} (\emph{kā}) + \textbf{\mr{य}} (\emph{ya}) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{काय}} \emph{kāy}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{काय}} (\emph{kāy}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) grows from the ancient interrogative stem \textbf{ka-}, from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — the very root behind English \textbf{wh-} words (\emph{what, who, when, where, why}) and Latin \emph{qu-} (\emph{quis, quid}). Marathi keeps the \textbf{k-} plainly across its whole question family: \textbf{\mr{काय}} (\emph{kāy}, what), \textbf{\mr{कोण}} (\emph{koṇ}, who), \textbf{\mr{कुठे}} (\emph{kuṭhe}, where), \textbf{\mr{का}} (\emph{kā}, why), \textbf{\mr{कसं}} (\emph{kasaṁ}, how — Chapter 10). Learn to hear that opening \textbf{k-} and you can spot a Marathi question coming.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
English \emph{wh-}, Latin \emph{qu-}, and Marathi \emph{k-} are three coats on one 5,000-year-old question-root — the family resemblance survives the different spellings.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kāy\textquotedblright{} — what
  \item three more Marathi \emph{k-} questions (\emph{koṇ, kuṭhe, kā})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do Marathi \emph{kāy}, English \emph{what}, and Latin \emph{quid} share? (One PIE question-root \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tumchaṁ nāv kāy āhe?]{\mr{तुमचं} \mr{नाव} \mr{काय} \mr{आहे}? (tumchaṁ nāv kāy āhe?) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-tumche-naav-kaay-aahe}



\begin{quote}
Now turn the question outward — ask someone else's name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the phrase, assembled}
\textbf{\mr{तुमचं}} (\emph{tumchaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}your,\textquotedblright{} neuter to match \emph{nāv}) + \textbf{\mr{नाव}} (\emph{nāv}, name) + \textbf{\mr{काय}} (\emph{kāy}, what) + \textbf{\mr{आहे}} (\emph{āhe}, is) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{तुमचं} \mr{नाव} \mr{काय} \mr{आहे}?} — literally \textquotedblleft{}your name what is?\textquotedblright{}, verb last.

The \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{} mirrors the \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} set you learned:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{माझं}} (\emph{mājhaṁ}) — my
  \item \textbf{\mr{तुमचं}} (\emph{tumchaṁ}) — your (respectful, from \emph{tumhī})
  \item \textbf{\mr{तुझं}} (\emph{tujhaṁ}) — your (familiar, from \emph{tū})
\end{itemize}

All three are shown here in the neuter, agreeing with the neuter \textbf{\mr{नाव}} (\emph{nāv}).

\begin{culture}
To a friend you would say \textbf{\mr{तुझं} \mr{नाव} \mr{काय} \mr{आहे}?} (\emph{tujhaṁ nāv kāy āhe?}), swapping the respectful \emph{tumchaṁ} for the familiar \emph{tujhaṁ} — the same \emph{tū / tumhī} choice of respect, now on the possessive.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tumchaṁ nāv kāy āhe?\textquotedblright{} — what's your name? (respectful)
  \item the familiar version (\emph{tujhaṁ nāv kāy āhe?})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the respectful and familiar \textquotedblleft{}your name\textquotedblright{} forms. (\emph{tumchaṁ} / \emph{tujhaṁ} — both neuter before \emph{nāv}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bheṭūn ānand jhālā]{\mr{भेटून} \mr{आनंद} \mr{झाला} (bheṭūn ānand jhālā) — \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-anand}



\begin{quote}
Names exchanged — now the warm close of a first meeting.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the phrase, assembled}
\textbf{\mr{भेटून}} (\emph{bheṭūn}, \textquotedblleft{}having met\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\mr{आनंद}} (\emph{ānand}, \textquotedblleft{}joy\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\mr{झाला}} (\emph{jhālā}, \textquotedblleft{}happened\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}having met {[}you{]}, joy happened.\textquotedblright{}} Marathi does not say \textquotedblleft{}I am pleased\textquotedblright{}; it says the joy itself \emph{occurred}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The heart of it is \textbf{\mr{आनंद}} (\emph{ānand}, \textquotedblleft{}joy, bliss\textquotedblright{}), pure \textbf{Sanskrit}: \textbf{\mr{आ}-} (\emph{ā-}, \textquotedblleft{}fully\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\mr{नन्द}} (\emph{nand}, \textquotedblleft{}to rejoice\textquotedblright{}). It is the \emph{ānanda} of the scriptural phrase \emph{sat-cit-ānanda} (\textquotedblleft{}being–consciousness–bliss\textquotedblright{}) — and one of the most common given names across India. So a Marathi speaker meets you and names the feeling \textbf{joy}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The verb \textbf{\mr{झाला}} (\emph{jhālā}, \textquotedblleft{}happened/became\textquotedblright{}) also carries gender — \emph{jhālā} by default here for the event \emph{ānand}. And \textbf{\mr{भेटून}} (\emph{bheṭūn}) is built on \textbf{\mr{भेटणे}} (\emph{bheṭṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet\textquotedblright{}) — a verb you will meet again in Chapter 11's goodbye, \emph{punhā bheṭū} (\textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}).
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bheṭūn ānand jhālā\textquotedblright{} — pleased to meet you
  \item what \emph{ānand} literally means (\textquotedblleft{}joy\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Literally, what does a Marathi speaker say when meeting you? (\textquotedblleft{}Having met you, \textbf{joy} happened\textquotedblright{} — \emph{bheṭūn ānand jhālā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 9 recap — introducing yourself}

\label{lesson:MR-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
Run the whole first exchange, atom by atom, then whole.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Marathi} & \textbf{Say it} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\mr{माझं} \mr{नाव} \mr{मीरा} \mr{आहे}. & \emph{mājhaṁ nāv Mīrā āhe.} & My name is Mira. \\
\mr{तुमचं} \mr{नाव} \mr{काय} \mr{आहे}? & \emph{tumchaṁ nāv kāy āhe?} & What's your name? \\
\mr{माझं} \mr{नाव} \mr{अरुण} \mr{आहे}. & \emph{mājhaṁ nāv Aruṇ āhe.} & My name is Arun. \\
\mr{भेटून} \mr{आनंद} \mr{झाला}. & \emph{bheṭūn ānand jhālā.} & Pleased to meet you. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — atoms banked this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{नाव}} (\emph{nāv}) — name; Sanskrit \emph{nāman} $\to$ English \textbf{name} (the \emph{m} softened to \emph{v} in Marathi).
  \item \textbf{\mr{माझं}} (\emph{mājhaṁ}) — my; root \emph{ma-} $\to$ English \textbf{me/my}; three genders \emph{mājhā/mājhī/mājhaṁ}.
  \item \textbf{\mr{आहे}} (\emph{āhe}) — is; Sanskrit \emph{ásti} (√as) $\to$ English \textbf{is}; the verb comes \textbf{last}.
  \item \textbf{\mr{तू} / \mr{तुम्ही}} (\emph{tū / tumhī}) — familiar / respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}; \emph{tū} $\to$ \textbf{thou}; courtesy-by-plural.
  \item \textbf{\mr{काय}} (\emph{kāy}) — what; PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}, the \emph{k-} question family.
  \item \textbf{\mr{आनंद}} (\emph{ānand}) — joy; Sanskrit \emph{ānanda}.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\end{itemize}

\section[śevaṭce sahā]{The last six, one chapter on}

\label{lesson:MR-R09-runway-tail-r2}



\begin{quote}
You closed the runway a chapter ago and have been introducing yourself since. Nothing to look at here — this is the first time those six are asked for cold.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Repair one group only. This is the first retrieval, not the last: the same six come back once at a durable gap, and once more at book distance near the end.

Which \emph{l} does Marathi keep that Hindi does not? (\textbf{The curled one.}) Which two sibilants are told apart only in spelling? (\emph{\textbf{śa\emph{ and }ṣa\emph{.\textbf{) {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Which vowel opens the word for one? (}}e\emph{.\textbf{) {[}PAUSE 2s{]} And how many written forms does the \emph{u} vowel have? (}Four — two letters and two marks.\textbf{)}}}}
\end{tcolorbox}
